query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as‐cast Co‐free FeNiCrMn, the dynamic response across temperature and strain-rate regimes is controlled by a rate‐dependent balance between dislocation generation (and, where applicable, deformation twinning) and dynamic recovery. At high strain rates, limited time for recovery promotes dislocation/twin accumulation that enhances yield strength and strain hardening, while at elevated temperatures enhanced dislocation mobility allows recovery that reduces strength but increases ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, single‐phase solid solution FeNiCrMn alloy with inherent dendritic solidification microstructure and minimal secondary phases
generation.intervention: Perform a systematic series of uniaxial tensile and/or compression tests on the as‐cast FeNiCrMn alloy across a range of strain rates (from quasi‐static ~10^(-3) s^(-1) to dynamic ~10^3 s^(-1)) and temperatures (cryogenic ~77 K, ambient ~300 K, and moderately elevated up to ~600 K).
generation.conditions: Tests should be conducted in a controlled atmosphere (to minimize oxidation) using standard load frames for low strain rates and a split-Hopkinson pressure bar (or equivalent dynamic setup) for high strain rates, with constant strain rate loads and isothermal conditions during each test.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and arrangement of dislocations (and any deformation twins) that form during dynamic loading.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures and high strain rates, the rate of dislocation (and twin) generation outpaces dynamic recovery, leading to accumulation that strengthens the material. Conversely, at higher temperatures, increased mobility promotes dynamic recovery (dislocation annihilation and rearrangement), which reduces yield strength despite high loading rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under quasi-static conditions at room temperature, baseline mechanical properties are observed; as strain rate increases at low temperatures, the yield strength and strain hardening rate will increase (due to dislocation/twin accumulation), whereas tests at elevated temperatures will show a reduced yield strength and increased ductility due to enhanced recovery.
generation.baseline: Mechanical behavior (yield strength, strain hardening rate, ductility) of the as-cast Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy measured under quasi-static loading at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to govern the dynamic response only in as-cast, homogenized FeNiCrMn alloys with minimal secondary phases, within the strain rate range of ~10^(-3) s^(-1) to ~10^3 s^(-1) and temperature range from cryogenic (~77 K) to moderate elevated temperatures (~600 K).
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of deformation twinning (as opposed to pure dislocation slip) in the low stacking fault energy regime of FeNiCrMn is not fully quantified and may vary with minor microstructural inhomogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of as-cast FeNiCrMn samples and subject them to controlled uniaxial tensile and/or compressive tests at varying strain rates (from ~10^(-3) s^(-1) to ~10^3 s^(-1)) and temperatures (77 K, 300 K, 600 K). After testing, perform TEM and/or EBSD characterization to quantify dislocation densities and any twin boundaries formed. Compare the mechanical data with the microstructural findings.
measurements: Yield strength and strain hardening rate as a function of strain rate and temperature
Post-deformation dislocation density and twin volume fraction via TEM/EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data do not show an increase in yield strength and strain hardening at high strain rates at low temperatures (i.e., no correlation with increased dislocation/twin density) or if the elevated temperature tests do not exhibit a reduction in strength associated with enhanced recovery, then the proposed dislocation/recovery controlled mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis paper investigates the effect of strain rate on the mechanical deformation and microstructural development of dual-phase AlCrFe2Ni2 high-entropy alloy during quasi-static and dynamic compression processes. It is revealed that the as-cast AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy is composed of a mixture of FCC, disordered BCC, and ordered B2 crystal structure phases. The alloy shows excellent compressive properties under quasi-static and dynamic deformation. The yield strength exceeds 600 MPa while the compressive strength is more than 3000 MPa at the compression rates of 30% under quasi-static conditions. Under dynamic compression conditions, the ultimate compression stresses are 1522 MPa, 1816 MPa, and 1925 MPa with compression strains about 12.8%, 14.7%, and 18.2% at strain rates of 1300 s−1, 1700 s−1 and 2100 s−1, respectively. The dynamic yield strength is approximately linear with strain rate within the specified range and exhibit great sensitivity. The strong localized deformation regions (i.e., adiabatic shear bands (ASBs)) appear in dynamically deformed samples by dynamic recrystallization due to the conflicting processes of strain rate hardening and heat softening.Keywords: high-entr

Unlike conventional metallic alloys, which are comprised of a base (solvent) and alloying (solute) elements, high entropy alloys (HEAs) are a class of structural alloys first introduced by Cantor et al. and Yeh et al. that consist of multiple principal elements in equiatomic or near equiatomic concentrations. Owing to their multi-principal element compositions, HEAs are characterized by unique combinations of properties, including mechanical strength,,, hardness,, and wear, and corrosion resistance. The use of multiple principal elements in far-from dilute concentrations unlocks infinite possibilities of combinations of properties and functionalities that are not typically found in conventional metallic alloys. Numerous recent studies on 3d transition metal HEAs, such as CoCrFeMnNi,, CoCrFeNi,, CoFeMnNi, CoCrMnNi, and Co0.25Cr0.1Fe2Mn1.35Ni1.3, have explored the impact of temperature,, grain size, alloy composition, strain rate, strain levels, and phase transformations, on the mechanical behavior of these alloys. The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, or so-called Cantor, alloy is a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase alloy that has been regarded as a model system to many single-phase HEAs.
